items.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I made some recordings with the Slam Stewart Quartet with John Collins on guitar... So I actually recorded with something called the Billy Taylor Trio... One of the records was made for Carl Records... It was with piano, bass, drums, and guitar... We spent a month in Haiti... John Collins on guitar

ctx.x: I believe there was an earlier recording you made with Charles Mingus, talk about that.

That was much later. In the records that we were looking through a moment ago, there was something… Walter Foots Thomas… those were the first records that I ever made in a professional sense. Those were the very first records I made and after that point I actually made some recordings… I tried to get a group together. I made some recordings with the Slam Stewart Quartet with John Collins on guitar, with Harold Doc West on bass, and Slam Stewart and myself. This was the group in which I had replaced Errol Garner.…

Thomas and all those guys were people that I worked with. Walter Foots Thomas had a studio on West 48th Street with Cozy Cole and they taught music. Cozy taught drum students and so forth. Cozy actually had originally had this arrangement with Gene Cruppa so at the time I was working with Walter, they were sharing an office space together, and so he introduced me to Cozy and he hired me, and Don Bias… Billy Taylor on bass, Billy Taylor who used to work with Duke Ellington, myself on piano, Tiny Grimes on guitar,…

items.title: 67250_John Collins oral history interview
items.q: And then I went into Birdland with Billy Taylor. We had a group, a quartet. Billy Taylor, Al McKibben, Jo Jones and myself.

ctx.x: Music Craft. And most of them were on Music Craft. And Billy left, and I'll tell you -- Billy got fired, really, and I never did appreciate it. Billy got married, and he went on his honeymoon and when he came back he didn't have a job. So I was furious with Slam because I'd left him. But Slam had heard a piano player, a girl and in Philadelphia by the name of Beryl Booker, who was a monster. And he literally paid Billy off, you know, and in order to keep this girl, you know, which we -- I enjoyed playing with…

She made everything right. She could play anything wrong and make it sound right. She was -- I don't think Beryl read. We would rehearse a tune, very intricate arrangement, this is with Slam Stewart, I'm still with Slam. And so we're going to do it tonight, and Beryl would get juiced. She drank quite a bit. So we probably did this
